title: CHAPTER 12: LATER MUGHALS & RISE OF REGIONAL POWERS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The death of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707 marked the rapid decline of Mughal central authority and paved the way for autonomous regional powers.
Regional polities during this period broadly categorized into Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Rebel States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats), and Independent Kingdoms (Mysore, Kerala).
In 1717, Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar issued a royal farman granting lucrative duty-free trading rights to the English East India Company in Bengal.
Devastating foreign invasions by Nadir Shah of Persia (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan severely crippled Mughal prestige and military power.
Internal factionalism among Mughal nobility (Turani, Irani, and Hindustani factions) prevented effective administrative governance.

blocks.content: The disintegration of the Mughal Empire created a political vacuum that facilitated the rise of autonomous regional powers and paved the way for British paramountcy.

rows: Former Mughal provinces that broke away as imperial control weakened, retaining Mughal administrative structures.
Nizam-ul-Mulk, Saadat Khan, Murshid Quli Khan
States established through armed rebellion against Mughal authority and expansionism.
Peshwas, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Churaman & Suraj Mal
States that expanded due to destabilization of imperial authority at the peripheries.
Hyder Ali, Tipu Sultan, Martanda Varma, Sawai Jai Singh

items: Founders of key successor states frequently asked: Nizam-ul-Mulk (Hyderabad, 1724), Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (Awadh, 1722), and Murshid Quli Khan (Bengal, 1717).
Farrukhsiyar's Farman of 1717 is often referred to as the 'Magna Carta' of the East India Company in Bengal.
Nadir Shah looted the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) and Koh-i-Noor diamond during the reign of Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' in 1739.
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) crushed Maratha ambitions to succeed the Mughals as the paramount imperial power in India.
